title: Believing Christ: The Parable of the Bicycle and Other Good News
author: Stephen E. Robinson
target_audience: Members of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints (LDS)
Christians interested in grace and salvation
Individuals struggling with perfectionism or feelings of inadequacy in spirituality
core_themes: Grace and the Atonement of Jesus Christ
Receiving, not just believing in, Christ
primary_purpose: To teach and reassure readers—especially Latter-day Saints—that salvation and acceptance by God come through Jesus Christ and His grace, rather than through personal perfection or works alone. The book seeks to help individuals fully accept the promises of the gospel and find peace and joy in Christ’s atonement.

structure_format.narrative_style: Personal and conversational, using parables, anecdotes, and scriptural analysis
structure_format.organization: Divided into chapters focusing on various aspects of faith, grace, and salvation, beginning with the Parable of the Bicycle and expanding into broader doctrinal discussions
features: Personal stories and analogies (notably the Parable of the Bicycle)
Direct addresses and applications to readers’ struggles

key_concepts_lessons: Christ’s Atonement bridges the gap between what we can do and what God requires—our personal efforts are necessary but not sufficient.
Salvation is not earned by perfect obedience, but given through the grace of Jesus Christ for those who believe and accept Him.
Believing Christ means trusting in His promises and accepting His help, not merely believing about Him.
Feelings of inadequacy or despair arise when we forget the role of grace.
Religious life is meant to bring hope and joy, not just pressure or guilt.
notable_features: The Parable of the Bicycle as a memorable analogy of grace
Focus on emotional relief for those burdened by perfectionism
Popular among LDS readers for its clarity and reassurance
Balanced discussion of faith and works in LDS doctrine
cultural_historical_context: Published in the early 1990s amidst ongoing theological discussion within the LDS community about the balance between grace and works. The book responded to a common cultural emphasis on perfection and self-reliance by offering a more grace-centered understanding in line with broader Christian doctrine.
reception_impact: Widely embraced by LDS readers and leaders, often recommended in talks and lessons
Sparked broader conversation within Mormonism about grace, faith, and salvation
The Parable of the Bicycle has entered LDS vernacular as a teaching tool
Critically considered transformative for members struggling with guilt or anxiety over personal worthiness
Some traditionalists initially questioned its downplaying of works, but it has since become influential in LDS soteriological discussions
comparable_titles: The Continuous Atonement by Brad Wilcox
The Infinite Atonement by Tad R. Callister
Grace Is Not God’s Backup Plan by Adam Miller
Mere Christianity by C.S. Lewis (for its faith/grace focus, outside LDS tradition)
